newsitem.title: FRANCE: Kurdish rebels say Iraqi troops preparing attack.
newsitem.headline: Kurdish rebels say Iraqi troops preparing attack.

text.p: Kurdish rebels in Iraq said on Thursday that elite Iraqi government troops were moving north from Baghdad to attack rebel positions and urged the United States and other nations to intervene.

"Iraqi Republican Guards are moving from the Baghdad area northward in preparation for imminent, hostile, offensive action against the Kurdish provinces of Arbil and Sulaymaniyah," the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK) said in a statement.
"We call upon the world, especially the United States, to prevent another onslaught by Saddam's forces against the people of Iraqi Kurdistan," said the statement, received in Paris.

"The makings of a new humanitarian disaster exist," the PUK added. "Faced with yet another Iraqi aggression, many Kurds will feel they have no choice but to flee to the mountains, joining the tens of thousands there already."
The PUK is trying to tighten the noose around the key northern city of Arbil and reverse losses in August to the pro-Baghdad Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP).

Later on Thursday, officials from the warring Kurdish factions are due to meet Assistant Secretary of State for Near Eastern Affairs Robert Pelletreau in Washington as part of U.S. efforts to end the inter-Kurdish conflict.
The United States leads a Western allied air force that shields the Kurds from any attack by the Iraqi forces of President Saddam Hussein.

The KDP captured Arbil six weeks ago with help from tank-led Iraqi troops. The United States fired missiles at military targets in south Iraq in response to the fall of Arbil, which ruined U.S. aid, military and intelligence efforts in northern Iraq.

The PUK has said that 6,000 of its fighters were gathering northeast of Arbil near a strategic road into the city. The group has wrested control of other main roads to Arbil, to the south and east, from the KDP. PUK leader Jalal Talabani has said he will not try to storm Arbil.
